content: The fortified cereal mix is specifically designed for infants and young children (IYC). For each of the three items analyzed, the nutrient profile is based on the nutrient content of the selected item. Non-target nutrients, such as vitamins and fatty acids, are also considered. Nutrient values for grains are calculated for raw or dry forms, adjusted using USDA retention factors for cooked forms like boiled maize flour and rice prepared with water. For wet or cooked forms, retention adjustments are applied. In the case of iron, the value for ferrous fumarate was used because the specifications for multiple micronutrient powders (MNP) and small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) indicate a mix of iron forms, with ferrous iron being the predominant type. Nutrient profiles for Optifood modeling focus on target vitamins, choline, and other essential nutrients. For example, values for vitamins A, B6, B12, thiamin, riboflavin, folate, and choline are provided per 100 grams, except for MNP and SQ-LNS, which have specific indications. Non-target nutrients, such as niacin and fatty acids (e.g., alpha-linolenic acid and linoleic acid), are also included. Niacin equivalents were calculated as the sum of niacin and tryptophan (divided by 60). Missing tryptophan data for approximately 30% of items were assessed, and it was determined that these gaps did not bias the mean niacin equivalent values. For fatty acids, data were available for fewer than 25% of food items. When specific values for alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) and linoleic acid (LA) were unavailable, undifferentiated values for 18:3 and 18:2 fatty acids were used. Nutrient values for grains were adjusted for raw or dry forms using USDA retention factors for cooked forms. The selection of parameters for Optifood modeling was guided by data analysis and supplemented with additional sources when necessary. Food patterns were modeled on a weekly basis, incorporating daily and weekly parameters such as median daily servings, maximum days of consumption per week, and maximum weekly servings for broad food groups. Methodological choices aimed to allow realistic yet generous amounts of nutrient-dense food subgroups. For example, starchy roots, tubers, and plantains were consumed by at least 20 children in datasets from eight countries, with median daily intakes ranging from 9 to 60 grams. The average of the two highest medians (~53 grams in Mexico and ~60 grams in Kenya) was used to set the parameter at 60 grams per day. Similarly, pork consumption among children aged 12–23 months was analyzed, with median daily intakes ranging from 15 to 27 grams. The median of the top two values (26 grams) was used, but additional data from Vietnam suggested a higher daily serving size of 35 grams, which was adopted. Breastfed infants presented unique challenges in modeling due to high milk intakes observed in some countries, which could displace breastfeeding. For example, milk intakes ranged from ~40 to ~240 grams per day across datasets from eight countries. The median among these values was 80 grams, and this informed the selected values for different age subgroups. Food patterns were developed to approximate real-world situations using data from Bangladesh, Malawi, and Mexico. Observed energy intakes were rescaled to align with fixed energy requirements (EERs) used in modeling. Breast milk intake was assumed to meet a fixed percentage of energy needs, with the remaining energy allocated to complementary foods and beverages. Excluded items, such as added sugars, broth, and plain tea, were proportionally redistributed across other food groups. In summary, the modeling process aimed to create realistic food patterns reflective of diverse settings while addressing nutrient gaps. The scenarios developed provide examples of broad dietary patterns with a basis in real-world data, though limitations in data availability and assumptions about feeding practices were acknowledged.
